Unit 2 A French Student in Dublin
변형문제 합본 · 전 37페이지
신목고 2-2 중간 · 세계문학
주제찾기
1 1번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
Meeting people from other cultures teaches us to notice both what we share and what we do not. A French student named Delphine flew to Dublin in March to stay with an Irish family for two weeks. She hoped to practise her English and to see something of the world beyond her own country. On the drive from the airport the rain came and went so quickly that a single hour felt like four seasons. The strange weather did not trouble her, because a lively Irish song was playing in the car. At the house the younger children looked as shy as she felt. She greeted them in Irish, and they answered in Irish too, stumbling over the words. After that small exchange the distance between them was noticeably shorter.
①the practical difficulties of travelling abroad as a teenager
②how a first greeting in a host country's own language eases strangeness
③the reasons Irish weather changes more often than French weather
④the advantages of learning English in an English-speaking country
⑤the role of traditional folk music in Irish family life
2 2번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
Delphine woke with a start on the morning of her first day at an Irish school. The house was in uproar as four children hunted for shoes and bags at once. Her host mother had already laid out a school uniform for her. It fitted well, though Dara had to knot the school tie for her. On the way she was pleased and frightened in equal measure. One of Dara's friends asked whether she was his girlfriend, and both of them blushed. At lunch she was astonished to find that pupils ate at their own desks. She did not follow every question the others asked, but the day was an enjoyable one.
①the strict discipline enforced in Irish secondary schools
②the difficulty of making friends in a foreign classroom
③the differences between French and Irish school uniforms
④a first school day in which small surprises outweigh the awkward moments
⑤the importance of learning a language before studying abroad

주제찾기
3 3번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
Lessons ended at four, and the pair were home by five. Her host mother called her to the table and announced that it was tea time. Delphine protested that she was hungry rather than thirsty. Dara laughed and explained that in Ireland the word means the evening meal. The dish itself joined French dried sausage to Irish potatoes under melted cheese. Delphine wished the family a good appetite, translating the phrase from her own language. The younger boys chuckled, and Dara told her the English form is different. She repeated the new expression and the meal went on.
①the best way to cook potatoes for a large family
②why French cooking is more elaborate than Irish cooking
③the health benefits of eating dinner earlier in the evening
④how children learn table manners from their parents
⑤how the same words carry different meanings across two cultures
4 4번 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
On her last full day the family took Delphine into the centre of Dublin. Her host mother explained who St. Patrick had been and why the date matters. He had brought Christianity to the island in the fifth century. Every seventeenth of March the country marks the day he died. The crowds wore green, pinned clovers to their coats and carried green banners. Green stands for the saint, and it is one of the three colours of the flag. At noon the bands set off along the winding streets, pipers first. Residents and visitors lined the route from beginning to end.
①a national holiday through which a people celebrate their own heritage
②the historical accuracy of stories told about early Irish saints
③the economic benefits that large parades bring to a capital city
④the reasons green became the most popular colour in Europe
⑤the training required to march as a traditional bagpiper

요지찾기
5 1번 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
Delphine travelled from Lyon to Dublin in March to spend a fortnight with the O'Briens. She wanted to improve her English, but she also wanted to widen her view of the world. The drive home brought drizzle, clear sky and heavy rain within a single hour. None of it bothered her, for a cheerful Irish folk song filled the car. Inside the terraced house, four younger children watched her without speaking. They looked shy, and a little nervous, exactly as she did. Then the guest offered a greeting in Irish, and the children replied in the same language. Awkward as the words were, everyone in the room felt closer once they were spoken.
①해외 생활은 언어 실력보다 날씨 적응이 더 어렵다.
②낯선 가정에 머무를 때는 예의를 갖추는 것이 가장 중요하다.
③민속 음악은 낯선 문화를 이해하는 가장 빠른 통로이다.
④교환학생은 도착 직후 현지 언어를 완벽히 익혀야 한다.
⑤서툴더라도 상대의 언어로 건넨 인사가 낯선 사이의 거리를 좁힌다.
6 2번 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
The whole household was hectic on the morning of Delphine's first school day. Ms. O'Brien checked that none of the children had crawled back into bed. A uniform was waiting for the guest, and Dara tied her school tie for her. She felt delighted and nervous at the same time as they walked to school. A boy asked whether she was Dara's girlfriend, and she denied it at once. Both of them were left looking thoroughly embarrassed. The rest of the day passed smoothly, apart from a lunch break spent at the desks. Much of the talk went over her head, and still she enjoyed herself.
①낯선 학교의 하루는 당황스러운 순간까지 포함해 새로운 경험이 된다.
②교복은 학생들 사이의 차이를 없애는 가장 효과적인 수단이다.
③외국어를 못 알아들으면 학교생활에 적응하기 어렵다.
④점심시간의 길이는 학업 성취도에 직접적인 영향을 준다.
⑤친구의 오해는 되도록 빨리 바로잡는 것이 좋다.

"It's tea time," Ms. O'Brien called, and Delphine assumed she meant a drink. She said she was starving, not thirsty, and Dara smiled at the mistake. In Ireland, he told her, 'tea' simply means dinner. The meal was a gratin of potatoes and French saucisson sec under cheese. Delphine wished everyone a good appetite, word for word from French. Dara's brothers chuckled at the phrase. They had understood her perfectly well; the English form is simply 'Enjoy your meal.' She said the new words aloud, and the evening carried on.
①외국어 학습은 어휘보다 발음이 우선이다.
②낯선 음식을 거절하지 않는 것이 손님의 예의이다.
③뜻이 통하더라도 그 언어에서 실제로 쓰는 표현은 따로 있다.
④가정식은 그 나라의 역사를 가장 잘 보여 준다.
⑤식사 시간은 나라마다 다르므로 미리 확인해야 한다.

Ms. O'Brien explained that St. Patrick was the patron saint of Ireland. He had brought Christianity to the country in the fifth century. March the seventeenth marks the anniversary of his death. On that day the Irish celebrate their heritage and their culture. The city centre filled with green clothes, clover pins and green banners. Dara added that green stands for the saint and appears in the national flag. Bands including traditional pipers marched through the winding streets at noon. Dubliners and tourists lined the route and were entertained from start to finish.
①축제의 규모가 클수록 그 나라의 전통이 잘 보존된다.
②종교 행사는 시간이 지나면 관광 상품으로 바뀐다.
③국기의 색은 그 나라의 지리적 특징에서 비롯된다.
④성 패트릭 데이는 아일랜드인이 자신들의 유산과 문화를 기리는 날이다.
⑤퍼레이드는 관광객 유치를 위한 도시 홍보 수단이다.

9 1번 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
In March a French student arrived in Dublin to spend two weeks with an Irish host family. Rain, sunshine and downpour followed one another so fast that an hour held every season. She was not troubled by it, since a cheerful folk song was playing on the car radio. The car stopped before a cosy terraced house where four younger children waited. They looked shy, and so did she. She spoke first, in Irish, though the language was not hers. The children smiled and answered awkwardly in the same tongue. From that moment the room felt warmer to everyone in it.
①Four Seasons in an Hour: Irish Weather Explained

③Eight Words in Irish: How a Greeting Broke the Ice
④The History of Irish Folk Music
⑤A Guide to Host Families in Dublin
10 2번 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
A beeping alarm pulled Delphine out of sleep on her first Irish school morning. Four children rushed about the house while their mother checked nobody had gone back to bed. She put on the uniform that had been left out for her. Dara had to help with the tie, which she had never worn before. At the gates a boy asked if she was his girlfriend, and both went red. Lessons went smoothly until the lunch break arrived. To her surprise, everyone stayed at their desks to eat. She missed much of what was said, and enjoyed the day all the same.

After a long day the two of them reached home at five. Ms. O'Brien announced tea time, and her guest pictured a cup of something hot. "I'm starving, not thirsty," Delphine said, puzzled. Dara explained that the word stands for dinner in Ireland. On the table was a gratin layering Irish potatoes with French sausage and cheese. Delphine offered the family a good appetite, straight out of French. The boys chuckled, and she learned to say 'Enjoy your meal' instead. Afterwards they talked over what they might do at the weekend.

The day before she left, Delphine went into Dublin with the O'Briens. It was the seventeenth of March, the anniversary of St. Patrick's death. The saint had carried Christianity to the island fifteen centuries earlier. Everywhere she looked the city had turned green. Clover-shaped pins, green glasses, green statues, green banners filled the streets. At noon the pipers led the bands along the winding roads of the capital. Afterwards the family walked her to St. Patrick's Cathedral across the river. Dublin, she learned, is a UNESCO City of Literature.

서술형 (본문 제시) · 1번
Meeting people from different cultures helps us develop understanding of other cultures and cultural awareness. We can discover similarities and differences between cultures and have more meaningful interactions with people around us. We can also build our respect and empathy for other people, and celebrate our differences as well as our similarities. In March, Delphine Froissart travelled from Lyon, France, to Dublin, Ireland, to spend two weeks with the O'Briens. She wanted to practise her English, but she also wanted to broaden her horizons by living abroad. Ms. O'Brien and her eldest son Dara met Delphine at Dublin Airport. On their drive home, it drizzled, cleared, and suddenly rained heavily. It was like having all four seasons in just an hour. Although quite new to Delphine, the changeable weather did not bother her as a cheerful Irish folk song “The Irish Rover” was playing on the radio. The car stopped at a cosy terraced house. Inside, Delphine met two younger boys and two younger girls. They looked shy and a little nervous. “Dia duit! (= Hello!) Is mise Delphine. (= I am Delphine.),” the guest said in Irish. They smiled shyly and replied awkwardly, “Deas bualadh leat! (= Nice to meet you.).” After greeting each other in Irish, they felt closer. Delphine unpacked her luggage and gave presents to Ms. O'Brien and the children. Finally arrived in Ireland. Somehow everything is different and new here! Ireland has fairly mild weather all year round for the most part. However, dressing for a day trip here can be a little tricky. You might wake up to glorious sunshine but end up facing a dramatic downpour by lunchtime, so the key is to be ready for anything. Wear plenty of thin layers so you can add or remove clothes as necessary, and carry an umbrella. One more thing: English is the primary language in Ireland. The nation also has its own language, Irish. Road signs are generally in both English and Irish languages.

Delphine woke up with a shock to a beeping sound. She was excited because this was her first day at school in Dublin. She was in Dara's class because they were both 16. The whole house was very hectic in the morning. All the kids rushed to get ready for school, with Ms. O'Brien checking that they had not gone back to sleep. Ms. O'Brien had a school uniform for Delphine. It suited her well although Dara had to help her with the school tie. Delphine was both delighted and nervous on the way to school. When they arrived, some of Dara's friends looked at Delphine and smiled. “Is this your girlfriend, Dara?” one of them asked. “I'm not his girlfriend!” Delphine quickly replied, feeling a bit embarrassed. Dara looked embarrassed, too. After that, the rest of the school day went smoothly except during the lunch break. Delphine was surprised to find students eat at their desks. Many kids asked Delphine about life in France. She didn't understand everything, but it was fun. Today I was at school. Dara's friends thought I was his girlfriend. :) I learned a few things. Uniforms are normal in Irish schools—with ties worn by both male and female pupils. Also, unlike in my school back home, students in most schools here bring their lunch and eat in the classroom, at their desks. The lunch break lasts an hour, just half of the two-hour break I have for lunch at school in France! It was a fun day.

It was a long day at school. Lessons finished at 4 p.m., and they got home at 5 p.m. “Hi, Delphine,” called Ms. O'Brien. “It's tea time.” “Tea time?” Delphine asked Dara. “But I'm starving, not thirsty!” Dara smiled. “Don't worry. 'Tea' means dinner in Ireland.” “Guess what's for tea,” Ms. O'Brien said to Delphine with a smile. “We're having potato gratin with saucisson sec and cheese. I thought the dish with French saucisson sec and Irish potatoes would be great.” Ms. O'Brien had cooked a gratin with layers of potato-saucisson mixture topped with cheese slices, breadcrumbs, and a large spoonful of butter. “Good appetite,” Delphine said—Dara's brothers chuckled. “Did I say something wrong?” Delphine asked. “No,” Dara answered. “We understood, but we don't say, 'Good appetite.' We say, 'Enjoy your meal.'” “Oh! Enjoy your meal,” Delphine said. After the meal, Dara discussed some things they could do over the weekend. Delphine was looking forward to seeing some of the sights of Dublin. Wednesday evening Ms. O'Brien cooked potato gratin with saucisson sec and cheese. I enjoyed the simple meal, and the potatoes were delicious. I'm glad Ms. O'Brien did not serve snails or frogs' legs as I'm French—it's a stereotype about the French, and young people like me dislike both foods. :)

서술형 (본문 제시) · 4번
The day before Delphine left, the O'Briens and Delphine visited Dublin's city centre to enjoy St. Patrick's Day. Ms. O'Brien explained that St. Patrick was the patron saint of Ireland who brought Christianity to the country in the 5th century, and that the Irish people celebrate their heritage and culture on March 17th, the anniversary of the saint's death. In the city centre, people wore green clothes with four-leaf clover-shaped pins and glasses. There were green rubber statues of St. Patrick, and streets were decorated with green banners. Dara said that green symbolises St. Patrick, and that green is one of the three colours in the Irish flag. When the St. Patrick's Day parade started at noon, many bands including traditional bagpipers marched along the winding streets of the Irish capital, entertaining Dubliners and tourists lining the parade route. Today, there was a sea of green everywhere. No wonder that Ireland is called the Emerald Island! After the parade, Ms. O'Brien and Dara took me to St. Patrick's Cathedral across the river. At the cathedral, Dara took a picture of me standing by the monument of Jonathan Swift, the famous author of Gulliver's Travels. With four Nobel Prize winners, numerous book festivals, and a world-class city library, it isn't surprising that Dublin is a UNESCO City of Literature.
